title: Fluid pressure and buoyancy: why things float
voiceInstructions: Speak as a warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Sound relaxed, lovely, welcoming and lightly playful, like explaining an interesting discovery to a student beside you. Use a gentle smile in the voice, expressive but subtle changes in pitch, natural contractions and conversational rhythm. Let curiosity and small moments of delight come through without exaggerated acting, baby talk, singing or a sales pitch. Avoid a flat, robotic or overly polished announcer cadence. Keep scientific terms precise. Slow down a little for equations, decimal numbers and unit conversions; separate the factors clearly. Give a brief natural thinking pause after a question, then explain with calm confidence. Do not add words or laughter that are absent from the script.

chapters.title: Pressure is force spread over area
points: A static fluid pushes perpendicular to a surface.
Pressure is measured in pascals: N/m squared.
200 N over 0.02 m squared gives 10,000 Pa.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Today, let's make sense of something you can feel: water pushing on you. We'll start with pressure, then use it to explain floating. Pressure tells us how much normal force acts per unit area. Normal here means perpendicular to the surface, not ordinary. So pressure equals force divided by area, when the pressure is uniform over that area. Imagine two hundred newtons spread over zero point zero two square metres. Divide two hundred by zero point zero two, and you get ten thousand pascals. Now spread the same force over twice the area. What happens? Give it a second. The pressure halves. Same force, more space to share it. A fluid at rest pushes perpendicular to the surfaces touching it. Pressure itself is a scalar, even though each pressure force has a direction. We'll also need density: mass divided by volume. Keep those two ideas separate. Density tells us how much mass occupies a volume; pressure tells us how intensely a surface is being pushed.

chapters.title: Deeper water means greater pressure
points: h is vertical depth below the liquid surface.
For constant density, the pressure increase is rho g h.
Water at 2 m depth: gauge pressure = 20,000 Pa when g = 10 m/s squared.
chapters.script: Why do your ears notice when you go deeper underwater? There's more water above you, and the pressure increases. Picture a stationary vertical column of liquid. The force from below must balance the force from above plus the column's weight. Divide that balance by the column's area, and the pressure increase becomes density times g times vertical depth. That's rho g h. At two metres below the surface of water, use density one thousand kilograms per cubic metre and g equal to ten. Multiply one thousand by ten by two: twenty thousand pascals. That's the pressure above the surface pressure, called gauge pressure when the surface is open to the atmosphere. If atmospheric pressure is given as one hundred thousand pascals, the absolute pressure is one hundred twenty thousand. A small but important extra step. Use vertical depth, not the distance along a sloping wall. And in the same connected stationary liquid of constant density, points at the same level have equal pressure. The container's shape doesn't get a vote.

chapters.title: Buoyancy comes from a pressure difference
points: Pressure on a submerged object's bottom exceeds pressure on its top.
Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.
Displacing 0.002 m cubed of water gives 20 N buoyancy for g = 10.
chapters.script: Now for the neat connection: pressure explains buoyancy. Imagine a block completely surrounded by still water. Its bottom is deeper than its top, so the upward pressure force on the bottom is larger than the downward force on the top. The side forces cancel horizontally. What's left is an upward resultant. Archimedes' principle says this buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. Not the weight of the object. That's the detail worth circling. Write buoyant force as fluid density times g times displaced volume. If the object displaces zero point zero zero two cubic metres of water, multiply one thousand by ten by zero point zero zero two. You get twenty newtons upward. If the object is partly submerged, use only its submerged volume, not its entire volume. We're assuming the fluid surrounds the wetted surfaces and the object isn't sealed against the bottom. For a rigid, fully submerged object in constant density water, going deeper doesn't by itself increase buoyancy: the displaced volume stays the same.

chapters.title: Floating finds its own submerged volume
points: With only weight and buoyancy, floating equilibrium requires equal forces.
For a uniform body: submerged fraction = rho(body)/rho(fluid).
A 600 kg/m cubed block in water floats with 60 percent submerged.
chapters.script: Let's float a uniform block whose density is six hundred kilograms per cubic metre in water of density one thousand. How much of it sits below the surface? Resist the urge to guess from the picture. Start with forces. For a freely floating block at rest, with no other vertical forces, buoyancy equals weight. Fluid density times submerged volume times g equals body density times total volume times g. Cancel g and rearrange. Submerged volume divided by total volume equals body density divided by fluid density. Six hundred divided by one thousand is zero point six. So sixty percent is submerged and forty percent is above water. Nice: we didn't need the block's size. We're neglecting air buoyancy and surface tension. If you add a load, the block must displace more water to support the extra weight. It settles lower until the forces balance, provided it can still float. A body's average density matters here. A hollow object can have a much lower average density than the material making its walls.

chapters.title: Apparent weight: a worked force balance
points: A hanging 3 kg object weighs 30 N for g = 10.
Fully submerged volume 0.002 m cubed gives buoyancy 20 N in water.
chapters.script: Let's finish with a spring balance. A three kilogram object hangs at rest and is fully immersed in water without touching the container. Its volume is zero point zero zero two cubic metres. Use g equal to ten and water density one thousand. What does the balance read? First, the gravitational weight is thirty newtons. Next, buoyancy is twenty newtons, using the displaced volume. Now draw the forces: tension upward, buoyancy upward, and weight downward. Since the object is at rest, tension plus buoyancy equals weight. The tension is ten newtons, and that's the balance reading. The object's mass hasn't changed. Water is providing part of the upward support. Here's your check: if someone reports minus ten newtons of tension, revisit the assumed equilibrium. An ordinary string cannot push downward to keep a buoyant object submerged. Before each fluid statics problem, ask: absolute or gauge pressure, total or submerged volume, and which forces actually act? Get those choices right, and the equations become much friendlier. Flowing fluids are a different chapter; today's results describe fluids at rest.

quiz.question: 200 N acts uniformly over 0.02 m squared. Pressure is:
At 2 m depth in open water, rho = 1000 and g = 10 in SI units. Gauge pressure is:
quiz.explanation: Gauge pressure = rho g h = 1000 x 10 x 2 = 20000 Pa.

quiz.question: An object displaces 0.002 m cubed of water. With rho = 1000 and g = 10, buoyancy is:
quiz.explanation: Buoyancy = rho g V = 1000 x 10 x 0.002 = 20 N.

quiz.question: A uniform block of density 600 kg/m cubed floats freely in water of density 1000 kg/m cubed. Submerged fraction is:
quiz.explanation: Balancing buoyancy and weight gives submerged fraction = 600/1000 = 0.6.
